clinicalPearls: A severe cutaneous adverse reaction characterised by the rapid eruption of numerous small, non-follicular sterile pustules on a background of oedematous erythema
The eruption begins in the flexures and on the face and spreads within hours, typically accompanied by high fever and a neutrophil leucocytosis
Onset is usually rapid, often within a couple of days of starting the responsible drug, most commonly certain antibiotics such as aminopenicillins and macrolides
The pustules are sterile, and swab cultures are negative, helping distinguish it from bacterial pustulosis
Resolution occurs quickly once the drug is withdrawn, characteristically followed by superficial desquamation of the affected skin
Histology shows subcorneal or intraepidermal spongiform pustules with dermal oedema and often eosinophils, aiding differentiation from pustular psoriasis
A key differential is generalised pustular psoriasis, which tends to run a more prolonged and recurrent course and may have a personal or family history of psoriasis
Management is prompt withdrawal of the culprit drug with supportive care, topical corticosteroids and monitoring for the uncommon systemic or organ involvement
reference.pathophysiology: Acute generalised exanthematous pustulosis is a T-cell-mediated (type IV) drug hypersensitivity reaction with a strong neutrophilic component. Drug-specific T lymphocytes are activated and, through release of neutrophil-recruiting cytokines and chemokines including interleukin-8 (CXCL8), interleukin-17 and granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor, drive massive accumulation of neutrophils into the epidermis to form sterile spongiform pustules. Interleukin-36 signalling is also implicated, providing a mechanistic overlap with pustular psoriasis. The rapid onset after drug exposure and swift resolution after withdrawal reflect the reactivation of primed drug-specific T cells and the transient nature of the ensuing sterile inflammatory response.
additionalDifferentials: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms with pustular features
Staphylococcal scalded skin or other pustular infections
additionalInvestigations: Detailed drug timeline identifying agents introduced in the days before onset
Skin biopsy showing subcorneal or intraepidermal sterile spongiform pustules with dermal oedema
Full blood count demonstrating neutrophilia and pustule swab confirming sterility
Assessment of liver and renal function to detect uncommon systemic involvement
Patch testing after recovery to help confirm the culprit drug
Application of a validated diagnostic scoring system to support the diagnosis
redFlags: High fever with extensive erythema and rapidly spreading pustulation
Evidence of internal organ involvement such as hepatic or renal dysfunction
Features overlapping with other severe cutaneous adverse reactions
Haemodynamic instability or signs of secondary infection
Failure to resolve after drug withdrawal, suggesting pustular psoriasis instead
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is generally favourable, with rapid clearance and desquamation within one to two weeks of stopping the culprit drug, although occasional cases with widespread disease, systemic involvement or in frail patients carry a higher risk of complications.
pitfalls: Mistaking the sterile pustules for a bacterial infection and delaying drug withdrawal while giving unnecessary antibiotics
Confusing it with generalised pustular psoriasis and misjudging the course and treatment
Failing to identify and stop the culprit drug promptly
references: British Association of Dermatologists guidance on severe cutaneous adverse reactions
management: Immediate withdrawal of the culprit drug, commonly an aminopenicillin or macrolide, as the definitive intervention
Topical corticosteroids and emollients to settle the pustular eruption, with antipyretics for fever
Reserve systemic corticosteroids for extensive or systemically involved disease
Skin care through the desquamative phase with prevention of secondary bacterial infection
Maintain fluid and electrolyte balance where the eruption is widespread
Monitor full blood count and liver and renal function for uncommon systemic involvement
Document the drug reaction, arrange patch testing after recovery, and counsel lifelong avoidance of the culprit and related agents
Dermatology referral to confirm the diagnosis and guide management
